{{smaller block|He is high in his owne imagination; . . . when hee goes, hee looks who looks; if hee finds not good store of ''vailers'' he comes home stiffe.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|vague|6686|vair}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|The strange and idill beggaris . . . are sufferit to ''vaig'' and wander throughout the haill cuntrey.
{{right|''Scotch Laws'', 1600, quoted in Ribton-Turner’s Vagrants [and Vagrancy, p. 350.}}

These small bodies, being hudled perforce one upon another, leave a large void space, to ''vague'' and range abroad.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 630.}}}}

'''vaguely''' (vāg′li), ''adv.'' In a vague, uncertain, or unsettled manner; without definiteness or distinctness.

'''vagueness''' (vāg′nes), ''n.'' The state of being vague, indefinite, unsettled, or uncertain; ambiguousness; indistinctness.
{{smaller block|Common language has, in most cases, a certain degree of looseness and ambiguity; as common knowledge has usually something of ''vagueness'' and indistinctness.
{{right|''Whewell'', Philos. of Inductive Sciences, I. xlviii.}}

There is a degree of ''vagueness'' about the use of the terms person and personality.
{{right|''H. B. Smith'', Christian Theology, p. 170.}}}}

'''vagus''' (vā′gus), ''n.''; pl. ''vagi'' (-jī). [NL. (sc. ''nervus'', nerve), < L. ''vagus'', wandering: see ''vague''.] '''1.''' The tenth cranial nerve, or wandering nerve, the longest and most widely distributed of the nerves of the brain, extending through the neck and thorax to the upper part of the abdomen. {{smaller|It supplies the organs of voice and respiration with motor and sensory fibers, and the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, and heart with motor influence. Its superficial origin is from the medulla, immediately in front of the restiform body and below that of the glossopharyngeal. It passes out of the cranial cavity through the jugular foramen, and accompanies the carotid artery in the neck to the thorax, where the nerves of the two sides differ in their course, that of the right side reaching the posterior surface of the esophagus and stomach, while that of the left goes to the anterior. It gives off very numerous branches, as the meningeal, auricular, pharyngeal, laryngeal, pulmonary, cardiac, gastric, etc., and forms intricate connections with other nerves of the cerebrospinal system, and with nerves of the sympathetic system. Also called ''pneumogastric'', ''par vagum'', and formerly ''second division of the eighth nerve of Willis''.}}

{{smaller block|The ''vagus'' nerve, which connects the brain with the viscera.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Education, p. 273.}}}}
'''2.''' In insects, the principal visceral or stomatogastric nerve, which originates in two parts in the head, beneath the bases of the antennæ, uniting in a ganglion below the cerebrum, and passing backward along the upper surface of the intestinal canal. {{smaller|In the thorax it divides into two parts, which give off numerous smaller nerves to all the viscera.—'''Trigonum vagi.''' Same as ''ala cinerea'' (which see, under ''ala'').—'''Vagus ganglion.''' See ''ganglion''.}}

'''Vahea''' (vä′hē-ä), ''n.'' [NL. (Lamarck, 1791), from the name of the tree in Madagascar.] A genus of apocynaceous plants, comprising a few (perhaps two) species formerly included in the genus ''Landolphia''. {{smaller|The name ''Vahea'' is also used by some in place of ''Landolphia'' for several other species which are important rubber-plants, as ''V''. (''L''.) ''Heudelotii'' of Senegal, ''V''. (''L''.) ''florida'' of West Africa, remarkable for the beauty of its abundant fragrant white flowers, and ''V''. (''L''.) ''Owariensis'' of Angola, which bears an edible, sweet and acidulous, pulpy fruit of the size of an orange.}}

'''vaich''', ''v. i.'' See ''rake''.

'''Vaidic, Vaidik''' (vā′dik), ''a.'' [< Skt. ''vāidika'', relating to the Vedas.] Same as ''Vedic''.

{{smaller block|The earliest religious utterances which have been preserved in Aryan literature are known as the ''Vaidik'' hymns.
{{right|''J. T. Wheeler'', Short Hist. India, p. 61.}}}}

'''vaig†''', ''v. i.'' A Scotch spelling of ''vague''.

'''vaik''', ''v. i.'' See ''rake''.

'''vail'''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''veil''.

'''vail<sup>2</sup>''' (vāl), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''vailen'', ''vaylen''; by apheresis from ''avail'': see ''avail''<sup>1</sup>.] To profit; benefit; avail: a poetical use.
{{smaller block|<poem>To hym not ''vaileth'' his preching,
Al helpe he other with his teching.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 5765.}}
<poem>''Vails'' not to tell what steeds did spurn,
Where the Seven Spears of Wedderburne
Their men in battle-order set.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., v. 4.}}}}

'''vail<sup>2</sup>''' (vāl), ''n.'' [By apheresis from ''avail''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] '''1†.''' Profit; gain; produce.
{{smaller block|My house is as ’twere the cave where the young outlaw hoards the stolen ''vails'' of his occupation.
{{right|''Marston, Jonson, and Chapman'', Eastward Ho, ii. 1.}}
His commings in are like a Taylors, from the shreds of bread, the chippings, and remnants of the broken crust: excepting his ''vailes'' from the barrell, which poore folkes buy for their hogs, but drinke themselues.
{{right|''Bp. Earle'', Micro-cosmographie, An old Colledge Butler.}}}}
'''2†.''' An unlooked-for or casual acquisition; a windfall. ''Tooke.''—'''3.''' Money given to servants by a visitor; a tip: usually in the plural. Also ''vale.''
{{smaller block|Why should he, like a Servant, seek ''Vails'' over and above his Wages? {{right|''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.}}
“Avails” is good old English, and the ''vails'' of Sir Joshua Reynolds’s porter are famous.
{{right|''Lowell'', Biglow Papers, 2d ser., Int.}}
On the smallest provocation, or at the hope of the smallest increase of wages, or still more of ''vales'', the servant threw up his place. {{right|''Lecky'', Eng. in 18th Cent., iv.}}}}

'''vail<sup>3</sup>†''' (vāl), ''v.'' [Also ''vale;'' by apheresis from obs. ''avale:'' see ''avale.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To let or cast down; let fall; lower; doff, especially in token of submission.

<poem>Then may’st thou think that Mars himself came down,
To ''vail'' thy plumes, and heave thee from thy pomp.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Greene'', Orlando Furioso.}}}}
<poem>None that beheld him but . . .
Did ''vail'' their crowns to his supremacy.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, ii. 3. 42.}}}}
<poem>Now ''vail'' your pride, you captive Christians,
And kneel for mercy to your conquering foe.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Marlowe'', Jew of Malta, v. 2.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To yield; give place; express respect or submission by yielding, uncovering, or otherwise; bow.

<poem>Because we ''vailed'' not to the Turkish fleet,
Their creeping galleys had us in the chase.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Marlowe'', Jew of Malta, ii. 2.}}
Every one that does not know cries, “What nobleman is that?” all the gallants on the stage rise, ''vail'' to me, kiss their hand, offer me their places.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, i. 3.}}}}

'''2.''' To drop; move down; take a lower position; slope downward.

{{smaller block|The same ships in good order ''valed'' downe the Riuer of Thames.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 288.}}
With all speed I ''vailed'' down that night ten miles, to take the tide in the morning.
{{right|''Capt. Roger Bodenham'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 33).}}}}

'''vail<sup>3</sup>†''' (vāl), ''n.'' [< ''vail''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] Submission; descent; decline.

<poem>Even with the ''vail'' and darking of the sun,
To close the day up, Hector’s life is done.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., v. 8. 7.}}}}

'''vailable†''' (vā′la-bl), ''a.'' [By apheresis from ''available.''] Profitable; advantageous. ''Smith,'' Commonwealth, ii. 4. (''Richardson.'')

'''vailer<sup>1</sup>''', '''vailing''', etc. See ''veiler,'' etc.

'''vailer<sup>2</sup>†''' (vā′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''vail''<sup>3</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who vails; one who yields or gives place in submission or deference.
{{smaller block|He is high in his owne imagination; . . . when hee goes, hee looks who looks; if hee finds not good store of ''vailers'' he comes home stiffe.
{{right|''Sir T. Overbury,'' Characters, A Golden Asse.}}}}

'''vaimure†''', ''n.'' Same as ''vantmure.''

'''vain''' (vān), ''a.'' [< ME. ''vain, vayn, vein, veyn,'' < OF. (and F.) ''vain'' = Pr. ''van, va'' = Cat. ''va'' = Sp. ''vano'' = Pg. ''vão'' = It. ''vano,'' < L. ''vanus,'' empty, void, fig. idle, fruitless; of persons, idle, deceptive, ostentatious, vain; perhaps orig. *''vacnus,'' and so akin to L. ''vacuus,'' empty: see ''vacuous, vacant.'' Some suggest a connection with E. ''wane, want, wan-''; but this is improbable. Hence (from L. ''vanus'') also E. ''vanish, vanity, vaunt, evanish, evanesce,'' etc.] '''1.''' Having no real value or importance; worthless; unsubstantial; empty; trivial; idle.
{{smaller block|<poem>But, O ''vain'' boast!
Who can control his fate?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' Othello, v. 2. 264.}}
''Vain'' matter is worse than ''vain'' words.
{{right|''Bacon,'' Advancement of Learning, i.}}
<poem>She . . . had never proved
How ''vain'' a thing is mortal love.</poem>
{{right|''M. Arnold,'' Switzerland, vi., Isolation.}}}}
'''2.''' Producing no good result; destitute of force or efficacy; fruitless; ineffectual; useless; futile; unavailing.

{{smaller block|It should be but a ''vaine'' thing, and counted but as lost laboure. {{right|''Levins'', Manip. Vocab. (E. E. T. S.), Pref., p. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|Give us help from trouble; for ''vain'' is the help of man.
{{right|Ps. lx. 11.}}}}

<poem>Let no man speak again
To alter this, for counsel is but ''vain''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 2. 214.}}}}

'''3.''' Light-minded; foolish; silly.

<poem>As school-maids change their names
By ''vain'' though apt affection.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 4. 48.}}}}

{{smaller block|For it is a ''vain'' thing to expect, in so open a condition as we live in here, that no cross Winds should blow upon us.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. x.}}}}

'''4.''' Proud of petty things or of trifling attainments or accomplishments; elated with a high opinion of one’s personal appearance, manners, or the like; courting the admiration or applause of others; conceited; self-complacent; also, proceeding from or marked by such pride or conceit: as, to be ''vain'' of one’s figure or one’s dress.

<poem>For to be conscious of what all admire,
And not be ''vain'', advances virtue higher.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Eleonora, l. 101.}}}}

{{smaller block|Mr. Holloway was a grave, conscientious clergyman, not ''vain'' of telling anecdotes, very learned, particularly a good orientalist. {{right|''T. Warton'', in Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 320.}}}}

{{smaller block|I never heard or saw the introductory words “Without vanity I may say,” etc., but some ''vain'' thing immediately followed. {{right|''Franklin'', Autobiog., p. 3.}}}} '''5.''' Showy; ostentatious; pretentious.
{{smaller block|Load some ''vain'' church with old theatric state.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iv. 29.}}}}

{{smaller|'''For vain†.''' Same as ''in vain.''}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Yea, my gravity,
Wherein—let no man hear me—I take pride,
Could I with boot exchange for an idle plume,
Which the air beats ''for vain.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., ii. 4. 12.}}}}

{{smaller|'''In vain,''' to no purpose; without success or advantage; ineffectually.}}
{{smaller block|Butt all that euer he spak it was ''in vayn.''
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3062.}}
''In vain'' they combated, ''in vain'' they writ.
{{right|''Prior'', Henry and Emma.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To take a name in vain.''' See ''name''<sup>1</sup>. ='''Syn. 1.''' Unreal, shadowy, dreamy, delusive, false, deceitful.—'''2.''' Bootless, abortive.—'''4.''' See ''egotism.''}}

'''vainful†''' (vān′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''vain'' + ''-ful.''] Vain; empty. ''Tusser'', Husbandry, Author’s Epistle, ii.

'''vainglorious''' (vān-glō′ri-us), ''a.'' [< ''vainglory'' + ''-ous.''] '''1.''' Filled with vainglory; glorying in excess of one’s own achievements; extravagantly elated; boastful; vaunting.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Vaine-glorious'' man, when fluttering Wind does blow,
In his light winges is lifted up to skye.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iii. 10.}}
The philosophers of his time, the flustring ''vain-glorious'' Greeks, who pretended so much to magnify and even adore the wisdom they professed.
{{right|''South'', Sermons, III. vi.}}}}
'''2.''' Indicating or proceeding from vainglory; founded on excessive vanity; boastful.
{{smaller block|Arrogant and ''vainglorious'' expression.
{{right|''Sir M. Hale.''}}
A ''vainglorious'' confidence prevailed, about this time, among the Spanish cavaliers.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 66.}}}}

{{smaller block|He discourses, in rather a ''vainglorious'' way, of himself as a poet.
{{right|''Ticknor'', Span. Lit., I. 249.}}}}

'''vaingloriously''' (vān-glō′ri-us-li), ''adv.'' With vainglory or inflated arrogance; boastfully.

'''vaingloriousness''' (vān-glō′ri-us-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being vainglorious.

'''vainglory''' (vān-glō′ri), ''n.'' [< ME. ''vaine glorie'', ''veingloire'', < OF. ''vaine gloire'', F. ''vaine gloire'', < L. ''vana gloria'', empty boasting: see ''vain'' and ''glory''.] Extravagant pride or boastfulness; tendency to exalt one’s self or one’s own performances unduly; inflated and pretentious vanity; vain pomp or show.

{{smaller block|''Vaine-glorie'' is for to have pompe and delit in his temporal highnesse, and glorie him in his worldly estate.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

{{smaller block|But for the fear of incurring the suspicion of ''vainglory'', he would have sung a psalm with as firm and cheerful a voice as if he had been worshipping God in the congregation.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}

'''vainglory''' (vān-glō′ri), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''vaingloried'', ppr. ''vainglorying''. [< ''vainglory'', ''n.''] To indulge in vain boasting. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|It would be idle and frivolous to mention these points for the sake of ''vain-glorying'' during the Jubilee year.
{{right|''Westminster Rev.'', CXXVIII. 485.}}}}

'''vainly''' (vān′li), ''adv.'' In a vain manner. {{smaller|Especially—(''a'') Without effect; to no purpose; ineffectually; in vain.}}
{{smaller block|In weak complaints you ''vainly'' waste your breath.
{{right|''Dryden''.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') In an inflated or conceited manner; proudly; arrogantly: as, to strut about ''vainly''. <poem>A stranger to superior strength,
Man ''vainly'' trusts his own.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Human Frailty.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Idly; foolishly; unreasonably; hence, erroneously; falsely.}}
{{smaller block|Which ''vainly'' I supposed the Holy Land.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 5. 239.}}
We haue sufficient to content our selues, though not in such abundance as is ''vainly'' reported in England.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 36.}}}}

'''vainness''' (vān′nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The state of being vain; ineffectualness; fruitlessness: as, the ''vainness'' of effort.—'''2.''' Empty pride; vanity.
{{smaller block|''Vainness'', a meagre friend to gratefulness, brought him . . . to despise Erona.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, ii.}}
Free from ''vainness'' and self-glorious pride.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., v., Prol.}}}}
'''3†.''' Foolishness; folly.
{{smaller block|<poem>O! how great ''vainnesse'' is it then to scorne
The weake!</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Visions of the World’s Vanity, l. 83.}}
<poem>I hate ingratitude more in a man
Than lying, ''vainness'', babbling, drunkenness.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 389.}}}}

'''vair''' (vãr), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''were''; < ME. ''vair'', ''vayre'', ''veir'', ''feir'', < OF. ''vair'', F. ''vair'' = Pr. ''vair'', ''var'', ''vaire'', fur of the ermine, < ML. ''varius'', also ''varis'', the ermine, < L. ''varius'', spotted, variegated: see ''various''. Hence ''vairy'', and the second element of ''miniver''.] '''1.''' A kind of fur in use in the middle ages. {{smaller|It is generally assumed to have been the skin of a small animal, such as the gray squirrel, of which the back is gray and the belly white. Compare ''miniver''.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
